title: Do bank boards focus adequately on risk?
venue: London School of Economics and Political Science Research Online (London School of Economics and Political Science)
abstract: Prior academic research on bank risk-taking has mostly concentrated on the role of board structure. However, board conduct and its relationship to risk-taking by banks has not received much attention. In this paper, we fill this gap by analyzing the minutes of board and risk management committee (RMC) meetings of 29 banks. We manually classify the issues into different categories, and code whether each issue has been deliberated at length. Among the issues tabled, risk accounts for only 11% while regulation and compliance account for the most (37%) followed by business strategy (35%). Only 20% of the issues are deliberated at length. The RMC meets infrequently and deliberates only 28% of the issues. Only 25% of the issues tabled in the RMC are forward-looking in nature. We interpret this evidence to imply that bank boards focus inadequately on risk and adopt a “box ticking” approach instead of focusing in spirit on risk oversight.

summary.oneLiner: Bank boards demonstrate inadequate focus on risk, often prioritizing compliance and business strategy over substantive risk oversight.
summary.overview: This study examines how bank boards manage risk by analyzing the meeting minutes of 29 banks. The authors find that boards spend significantly more time on regulation, compliance, and business strategy than on risk management. Furthermore, the majority of board discussions are not deliberated at length, and many risk-related discussions lack a forward-looking perspective. The authors conclude that boards tend to adopt a "box-ticking" approach rather than engaging in deep, meaningful oversight of bank risks.
summary.question: Do bank boards focus adequately on risk management?
summary.method: Manual coding and analysis of board and risk management committee meeting minutes.
findings: Risk-related issues account for only 11% of the topics discussed by bank boards.
Regulation and compliance (37%) and business strategy (35%) dominate board agendas.
Only 20% of tabled board issues receive lengthier deliberation.
Risk management committees meet infrequently and deliberate only 28% of the issues presented to them.
Only 25% of issues tabled in risk management committees are forward-looking.
summary.whyItMatters: The findings suggest that current governance practices in banks may be insufficient, as boards appear to prioritize procedural compliance over genuine risk oversight, which could impact institutional stability.
